content: The frequency of dental check-ups and their impact on oral health remains a topic of debate. Recommendations for optimal recall intervals differ across countries and healthcare systems. However, in many high-income countries, general dental practitioners have traditionally recommended check-ups every six months. This review aimed to determine the ideal interval for dental check-ups in primary care settings, updating previous versions published in 2005, 2007, and 2013. To gather evidence, databases such as the Cochrane Oral Health Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase were searched up to January 2020. Additional searches were conducted in the US National Institutes of Health Trials Registry and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effects of different dental recall intervals in primary care were included. Data were extracted and analyzed independently by two reviewers, and the certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Two studies involving 1,736 participants were included. One study, conducted in Norway, focused on individuals under 20 years of age who regularly attended dental appointments. It compared 12-month and 24-month recall intervals over a two-year period. The second study, conducted in the UK, involved adults who had attended the dentist at least once in the previous two years. It compared 6-month, 24-month, and risk-based recall intervals over a four-year period. The primary outcomes assessed were dental caries, gingival bleeding, and oral-health-related quality of life. Neither study evaluated potential adverse effects of different recall intervals. 24-Month vs. 12-Month Recall Intervals (2-Year Follow-Up) For children aged 3 to 5 years with primary teeth, the difference in the increment of decayed, missing, and filled tooth surfaces (dmfs) between 24-month and 12-month recall intervals was 0.90 (95% CI: -0.16 to 1.96). For adolescents aged 16 to 20 years with permanent teeth, the difference in the increment of decayed, missing, and filled surfaces (DMFS) was 0.86 (95% CI: -0.03 to 1.75). However, the evidence was of very low certainty, making it unclear whether there is a meaningful difference in caries experience between the two recall intervals. Other clinical outcomes were not assessed in this trial. Risk-Based vs. 6-Month Recall Intervals (4-Year Follow-Up) High-certainty evidence from one trial involving adults showed little to no difference between risk-based and 6-month recall intervals in the following outcomes: Number of tooth surfaces with any caries (ICDAS 1 to 6): Mean difference (MD) 0.15 (95% CI: -0.77 to 1.08). Proportion of sites with gingival bleeding: MD 0.78% (95% CI: -1.17% to 2.73%). Oral-health-related quality of life (measured by OHIP-14 scores): MD -0.35 (95% CI: -1.02 to 0.32). Moderate-certainty evidence suggested little to no difference in the prevalence of moderate to extensive caries (ICDAS 3 to 6) between the two groups (Risk Ratio [RR] 1.04, 95% CI: 0.99 to 1.09). 24-Month vs. 6-Month Recall Intervals (4-Year Follow-Up) Moderate-certainty evidence from one trial involving adults indicated little to no difference between 24-month and 6-month recall intervals in the following outcomes: Number of tooth surfaces with any caries: MD -0.60 (95% CI: -2.54 to 1.34). Percentage of sites with gingival bleeding: MD -0.91% (95% CI: -5.02% to 3.20%). Low-certainty evidence suggested little to no difference in the prevalence of moderate to extensive caries (RR 1.05, 95% CI: 0.92 to 1.20). High-certainty evidence showed no significant difference in oral-health-related quality of life (MD in OHIP-14 scores: -0.24, 95% CI: -1.55 to 1.07). Risk-Based vs. 24-Month Recall Intervals (4-Year Follow-Up) Moderate-certainty evidence from one trial involving adults suggested little to no difference between risk-based and 24-month recall intervals in the following outcomes: Prevalence of moderate to extensive caries: RR 1.06 (95% CI: 0.95 to 1.19). Number of tooth surfaces with any caries: MD 1.40 (95% CI: -0.69 to 3.49). High-certainty evidence indicated no significant difference in the percentage of sites with gingival bleeding (MD -0.07%, 95% CI: -4.10% to 3.96%) or in oral-health-related quality of life (MD in OHIP-14 scores: -0.37, 95% CI: -1.69 to 0.95). Authors' Conclusions For adults attending dental check-ups in primary care settings, there is high-certainty evidence that risk-based and 6-month recall intervals result in little to no difference in the number of tooth surfaces with caries, gingival bleeding, and oral-health-related quality of life over a four-year period. Moderate-certainty evidence suggests little to no difference in the prevalence of moderate to extensive caries between these recall strategies. Similarly, when comparing 24-month recall intervals with either 6-month or risk-based intervals, moderateto high-certainty evidence indicates little to no difference in these outcomes over a four-year period. However, the evidence regarding recall intervals for children and adolescents remains uncertain. Neither of the included trials assessed adverse effects associated with different recall strategies.
